o: We must transpose a sentence: word i occupies column i, and row r of the output contains the r-th character of every word (a space if that word is shorter). Trailing spaces are stripped from each output row. For "HOW ARE YOU": column 0 gives H,O,W; column 1 gives A,R,(space→stripped at end); column 2 gives Y,O,U, producing ["HAY","ORO","WEU"]. For "TO BE OR NOT TO BE", the third row is '   T' because only the 4th word (NOT) has a third character. With |s| ≤ 200 there are at most ~100 words and ~100 rows, so any straightforward simulation is fast enough.
k: The answer is simply the matrix transpose of the words padded with spaces.
Trailing spaces in each row must be stripped before adding to the result.
Rows only need to go up to the length of the longest word.

a.i: Pad every word with spaces up to the maximum word length, then read column by column and strip trailing spaces. This directly mirrors the visual layout described in the problem.
s: Split s into words and compute maxLen = max word length.
For each column c from 0 to maxLen-1, build a string taking word[c] if c < len(word), else a space.
Strip trailing spaces from each column string.
Append non-empty strings to the answer list.
a.t: O(n·m) where n is the number of words and m the longest word length — we build each of the m columns by scanning all n words.
a.sp: O(n·m) for the output plus O(n·m) transiently for padded columns.

a.i: Instead of building full padded columns, iterate over s once, tracking the current word index and character position within it. Append each character to its column's builder, padding shorter columns with spaces as needed when a later word extends past them. This avoids re-scanning all words per column.
s: Initialize an empty list of StringBuilder columns and counters wordIdx = 0, pos = 0.
Scan each character of s: on a space, increment wordIdx and reset pos to 0.
Otherwise, ensure the columns list has an entry at index pos (padding earlier entries with spaces to their final lengths), append the char to columns[pos], and increment pos.
Convert all builders to strings and strip trailing spaces.
a.t: O(|s|) — each input character is processed exactly once; padding work is bounded by total output size.

w: In an interview, start with Approach 1 since it maps directly onto the mental picture of a padded grid; mention Approach 2 as a one-pass refinement if asked to avoid redundant scans. Common pitfalls: forgetting to strip trailing spaces (Example 2 fails), assuming all words have equal length, and off-by-one errors when a later word is longer than earlier ones (columns must be back-filled with spaces). Edge cases: single word (output is just its characters), single character words. Follow-ups might ask to do it without extra padding memory or to handle multiple/leading spaces, which the one-pass approach handles naturally.
